title: Practice problems combining multiple C concepts
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its relevant rules.
Trace the example and justify its behaviour.
Identify important assumptions and failure cases.
Apply the concept in a reviewed and tested exercise.

understand.concept: Integrated practice requires learners to combine data types, decisions, loops, functions, arrays, pointers, structures or file handling in one solution. The problem should identify which concepts are required and which design choices remain open.
understand.whyItMatters: Real programs rarely use one isolated language feature. Integrated problems reveal whether learners can select and combine concepts appropriately.
understand.analogy: Treat standards, interfaces and release steps as explicit contracts that make assumptions visible.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace the C standard, implementation documentation or project-specific requirements.

explain.narrative:
Integrated practice requires learners to combine data types, decisions, loops, functions, arrays, pointers, structures or file handling in one solution. The problem should identify which concepts are required and which design choices remain open.

State assumptions and constraints, consult the applicable standard or tool documentation, and verify the result with appropriate compiler diagnostics and tests. Separate portable guarantees from implementation-specific behaviour.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The function combines a structure, array traversal and arithmetic aggregation. A production version must validate nonnegative values and guard multiplication and addition against overflow.

practise.guidedTask: Identify every C concept used in the example.
practise.independentTask: Design a small stock report using structures, functions, arrays and input validation. State the numeric limits and error policy.
hints: Break a combined task into smaller functions before coding.
Check overflow in intermediate calculations, not only the final result.
Write tests for empty, typical and extreme inputs.
